# Ibn Taymiyya on the Record of His Own School

Taqi al-Din Ahmad ibn Taymiyya (661-728 AH) is remembered today as a renewer of the Hanbali school and the ancestor of a movement. His own tradition tells a fuller story. The biographical dictionaries, travel diaries, court records, and fatwa collections document it. The writers are the scholars who sat in his circles, judged his cases, and buried him. The talent is conceded first, in the words of his own contemporaries and students. Then the record turns. The creed incidents repeatedly put him before councils of judges. The grave-visitation ruling sent him to his final prison. There is a signed recantation of 707 and a proclamation over Damascus. Later authorities of the Shafi'i school and one Hanbali of his own line also recorded verdicts against him.

Every quotation below is cited to a Sunni source. Where a report survives only in a relay, the relay is named. Where the record conflicts, the conflict is stated.


## The Talent Conceded

- **Source:** al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.178
- **Speaker:** Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi, the era's foremost grammarian
- **Claim:** he praised Ibn Taymiyya in improvised verse, then broke with him permanently over one discourtesy about Sibawayh

Abu Hayyan of Granada met Ibn Taymiyya in Cairo and praised him in improvised verse. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani preserves both the poem and what followed it in the authoritative biographical dictionary of the eighth century.

> [!note]- Abu Hayyan's praise, in Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.178
> لما اتانا تقي الدين لاح لنا * * داع إلى اللّه فرد ما له وزر
> على محياه من سيما الأولى صحبوا * * خير البرية نور دونه القمر
> حبر تسربل منه دهره حبرا * * بحر تقاذف من أمواجه الدرر
> قام ابن تيمية في نصر شرعتنا * * مقام سيدتيم إذ عصت مضر
> واظهر الحق إذ آثاره اندرست * * واخمد الشر إذ طارت له شرر
> كنا نحدث عن حبر يجئ بها (1) * أنت الامام الذي قد كان ينتظر 
> ثم دار بينهما كلام فجرى ذكر سيبويه فاغلظ ابن تيمية القول في سيبويه فنافره أبو حيان وقطعه بسببه ثم عاد ذا ماله وصير ذلك ذنبا لا يغفر قال وحج ابن المحب سنة 34 فسمع من أبى حيان انا شيد فقرأ عليه هذه الأبيات فقال قد كشطتها من ديواني ولا اذكره بخير فسأله عن السبب
>
> "When Taqi al-Din came to us, there appeared to us a caller to God, singular and bearing no burden.
>
>
> On his face were the marks of those who accompanied the best of created beings, a light before which the moon is dim.
>
>
> A learned scholar whose age clothed him in learning, a sea whose waves cast forth pearls.
>
>
> Ibn Taymiyya rose to support our law as Sayyid Tamim rose when Mudar rebelled.
>
>
> He made the truth manifest after its traces had been effaced, and he extinguished evil after its sparks had flown.
>
>
> We used to speak of a learned scholar who would come with it. You are the imam who had been awaited.
>
>
> Then words passed between them, and Sibawayh was mentioned. Ibn Taymiyya spoke harshly about Sibawayh, so Abu Hayyan broke with him and cut him off because of it. He then went back on all that he had said and made it an unforgivable sin. He said that Ibn al-Muhibb performed the pilgrimage in the year 734 and heard from Abu Hayyan that he had composed these verses. He recited them to him, and Abu Hayyan said, "I have erased them from my collected poems, and I do not mention him favorably." He asked him about the reason."

The poem is the measure of the man at his best. The same entry preserves the sequel. Words passed between the two men, the grammarian Sibawayh was mentioned, and Ibn Taymiyya spoke harshly of him. Abu Hayyan broke with him over that single discourtesy, crossed the verses out of his collected poems, and said he would not mention him favorably again. A mind that could win Abu Hayyan's verse could also lose him with a sentence.


## The Minbar in Damascus

- **Source:** Rihlat Ibn Batuta, vol.1, pp.316-317
- **Speaker:** Ibn Batuta, who states he was present in Damascus
- **Claim:** Ibn Taymiyya illustrated the divine descent from the minbar step, a Maliki jurist who objected was beaten by the crowd, and the judges' protest reached the sultan

The traveler Ibn Batuta passed through Damascus and left a portrait in his Rihla.

> [!note]- Ibn Batuta, Rihlat Ibn Batuta (Tuhfat al-Nuzzar), vol.1, p.316
> وكان بدمشق من كبار الفقهاء الحنابلة تقي الدين ابن تيمية (221) كبير الشأن يتكلم في الفنون إلا أن في عقله شيئا ! وكان أهل دمشق يعظمونه أشد التعظيم ويعظهم على المنبر ، وتكلم مرة بأمر أنكره الفقهاء ورفعوه إلى الملك الناصر فأمر بإشخاصه إلى القاهرة وجمع القضاة والفقهاء بمجلس الملك الناصر وتكلم شرف الدين الزواوي المالكي (222) ، وقال :
> إن هذا الرجل قال : كذا ، وعدّد ما أنكر على ابن تيمية ، وأحضر العقود بذلك ووضعها بين يدي قاضي القضاة وقال قاضي القضاة لابن تيمية : ما تقول ؟ قال : لا إلاه إلا الله ، فأعاد عليه فأجاب بمثل قوله ، فأمر الملك الناصر بسجنه فسجن أعواما ، وصنف في السجن كتابا
>
> "In Damascus there was among the leading Hanbali jurists Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya, a man of great standing who spoke on various disciplines, except that there was something wrong with his mind. The people of Damascus held him in the highest reverence, and he preached to them from the minbar. On one occasion he spoke about a matter that the jurists condemned and brought before al-Malik al-Nasir. He ordered that Ibn Taymiyya be brought to Cairo. The judges and jurists were assembled in the council of al-Malik al-Nasir, and Sharaf al-Din al-Zawawi the Maliki spoke and said, "This man said such and such," and listed what had been condemned in Ibn Taymiyya. He produced the documents concerning this and placed them before the Chief Judge. The Chief Judge said to Ibn Taymiyya, "What do you say?" He said, "There is no god but God." He repeated the question, and Ibn Taymiyya answered in the same way. Al-Malik al-Nasir ordered him imprisoned, so he was imprisoned for years. While in prison, he composed a book."

The portrait is double-edged, and it says so itself. Ibn Taymiyya was among the leading Hanbali jurists of Damascus, a man of great standing who spoke on the sciences. There was something wrong with his mind. Ibn Batuta then records what he says he witnessed on a Friday.

> [!note]- Ibn Batuta, Rihlat Ibn Batuta (Tuhfat al-Nuzzar), vol.1, p.317
> لاقه إلى أن وقع منه مثل ذلك ثانية ، وكنت إذ ذاك بدمشق (223) فحضرته يوم الجمعة وهو يعظ الناس على منبر الجامع ويذكّرهم فكان من جملة كلامه أن قال : إن الله ينزل إلى سماء الدنيا كنزولي هذا ، ونزل درجة من درج المنبر ، فعارضه فقيه مالكي يعرف بابن الزهراء وأنكر ما تكلم به ، فقامت العامة إلى هذا الفقيه وضربوه بالأيدي والنعال ضربا كثيرا حتى سقطت عمامته وظهر على رأسه شاشية حرير ، فأنكروا عليه لباسها واحتملوه إلى دار عز الدين بن مسلّم قاضي الحنابلة فأمر بسجنه وعزره بعد ذلك ، فأنكر فقهاء المالكية والشافعية ما كان من تعزيره ورفعوا الأمر إلى ملك الأمراء سيف الدين تنكيز (224) وكان من خيار الأمراء وصلحائهم ، فكتب إلى الملك الناصر بذلك وكتب عقدا شرعيا على ابن تيمية بأمور منكرة منها : أن المطلّق بالثلاث في كلمة واحدة لا تلزمه إلا طلقة واحدة ، (225) ومنها أن المسافر الذي ينوي بسفره زيارة القبر الشريف زاده الله طيبا لا يقصر الصلاة ، وسوى ذلك مما يشبهه ، وبعث العقد إلى الملك الناصر فأمر بسجن ابن تيمية بالقلعة فسجن بها حتى مات في السجن .
> 
> ذكر مدارس دمشق
> إعلم أن للشافع
>
> "until the like of that occurred from him a second time. At that time I was in Damascus, and I attended him on Friday while he was preaching and reminding the people from the minbar of the congregational mosque. Among his words was his statement, "God descends to the lowest heaven as I descend in this way," and he descended one step of the minbar. A Maliki jurist known as Ibn al-Zahra objected to him and condemned what he had said. The common people rose against this jurist and struck him greatly with their hands and sandals until his turban fell off and a silk cap appeared on his head. They condemned him for wearing it and carried him to the house of Izz al-Din Ibn Muslim, the Hanbali judge. He ordered him imprisoned and afterward disciplined him. The Maliki and Shafi'i jurists condemned his having been disciplined and referred the matter to the commander of the emirs, Sayf al-Din Tankiz, who was among the best and most righteous of the emirs. He wrote to al-Malik al-Nasir about this and drew up a legal document against Ibn Taymiyya concerning objectionable matters, among them that a man who pronounces a threefold divorce in one utterance incurs only one divorce, and among them that a traveler whose purpose in traveling is to visit the Noble Grave, may God increase it in goodness, does not shorten the prayer, along with other similar matters. He sent the document to al-Malik al-Nasir, who ordered Ibn Taymiyya imprisoned in the Citadel. He remained imprisoned there until he died in prison.
>
>
> Mention of the schools of Damascus
> Know that the Shafi'is"

On this report, Ibn Taymiyya, preaching on the descent of God, descended one step of the minbar to illustrate the manner of the descent. The Maliki jurist Ibn al-Zahra objected from the congregation. The crowd beat the objector with hands and sandals until his turban fell. The Hanbali judge of Damascus then imprisoned the objector and had him disciplined. The Maliki and Shafi'i jurists carried the protest to the governor of Syria, Tankiz. The modern editors of the Rihla note a chronological difficulty in the report. One commentator suggested the scribe embellished it. The report stands as the traveler recorded it, with that doubt attached.


## The Ruling on Visiting Graves

- **Source:** Majmu' al-Fatawa, vol.27, p.27
- **Speaker:** Ibn Taymiyya, citing Ibn Aqil and a group of the scholars
- **Claim:** travel to visit the graves of the prophets is disobedience, and the traveler does not shorten his prayer on that journey

The ruling that put Ibn Taymiyya in his final prison was his own, recorded in his own collected fatwas.

> [!tip]- Ibn Taymiyya, Majmu' al-Fatawa, vol.27, p.27
> بِأَنَّ الْمُسَافِرَ لِزِيَارَةِ قُبُورِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ عَلَيْهِمْ السَّلَامُ وَغَيْرِهَا لَا يَقْصُرُ الصَّلَاةَ فِي هَذَا السَّفَرِ ؛ لِأَنَّهُ مَعْصِيَةٌ لِكَوْنِهِ مُعْتَقِداً أَنَّهُ طَاعَةٌ وَلَيْسَ بِطَاعَةِ وَالتَّقَرُّبُ إلَى اللَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ بِمَا لَيْسَ بِطَاعَةِ هُوَ مَعْصِيَةٌ ؛ وَلِأَنَّهُ نَهَى عَنْ ذَلِكَ وَالنَّهْيُ يَقْتَضِي التَّحْرِيمَ .
> وَرَخَّصَ بَعْضُ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ فِي السَّفَرِ لِزِيَارَةِ الْقُبُورِ كَمَا ذَكَرَ أَبُو
>
> "A traveler who travels to visit the graves of the prophets, peace be upon them, and others does not shorten the prayer during this journey, because it is a sin. This is because he believes it to be an act of obedience, when it is not an act of obedience. Seeking nearness to God, Mighty and Majestic, through what is not an act of obedience is a sin. It is also because he prohibited that, and a prohibition entails forbiddance.
>
>
> Some later scholars permitted traveling to visit graves, as Abu mentioned"

The reasoning is stated plainly. A traveler who sets out to visit the graves of the prophets believes he is performing an act of obedience, and the act is not one. Seeking nearness to God through what is not obedience is disobedience, and the prohibition entails forbiddance. Ibn Taymiyya cites earlier authorities for the ruling and notes that some later scholars permitted the travel. The Arabic excerpt breaks off inside the name of Ibn Aqil, the authority the fatwa is citing. Elsewhere in the same volume, in the passage at vol.27, p.253, he denounces as slander the summary claim that he forbids visiting the Prophet's grave and traveling to it. Both texts are his. On this record the operative ruling is the first, and the governor's dossier itemized it when the final imprisonment came.

> [!note]- Ibn Batuta, Rihlat Ibn Batuta, vol.1, p.317
> فكتب إلى الملك الناصر بذلك وكتب عقدا شرعيا على ابن تيمية بأمور منكرة منها : أن المطلّق بالثلاث في كلمة واحدة لا تلزمه إلا طلقة واحدة ، (225) ومنها أن المسافر الذي ينوي بسفره زيارة القبر الشريف زاده الله طيبا لا يقصر الصلاة ، وسوى ذلك مما يشبهه ، وبعث العقد إلى الملك الناصر فأمر بسجن ابن تيمية بالقلعة فسجن بها حتى مات في السجن .
> 
> ذكر مدارس دمشق
> إعلم أن للشافعية بدمشق جملة من المدارس أعظمها العادلية (226) ، وبها يحكم قاضي القضاة ، وتقابلها المدرسة الظاهرية (227) وبها قبر الملك الظاهر ، وبها جلوس نواب
>
> "He wrote to al-Malik al-Nasir about this and drew up a legal document against Ibn Taymiyya concerning objectionable matters, among them that a man who pronounces a threefold divorce in one utterance incurs only one divorce, and among them that a traveler whose purpose in traveling is to visit the Noble Grave, may God increase it in goodness, does not shorten the prayer, along with other similar matters. He sent the document to al-Malik al-Nasir, who ordered Ibn Taymiyya imprisoned in the Citadel. He remained imprisoned there until he died in prison.
>
>
> Mention of the schools of Damascus
> Know that the Shafi'is in Damascus have a number of schools, the greatest of which is the Adiliyya. The Chief Judge gives judgment there. Opposite it is the Zahariyya school, in which is the grave of al-Malik al-Zahir, and there is the seat of the deputies"

The dossier Tankiz, governor of Syria, sent to Sultan al-Nasir named the rulings as errors. The threefold divorce counted as one. The pilgrim who intends the visit of the grave does not shorten his prayer. The order that followed confined Ibn Taymiyya to the citadel of Damascus, where he remained until he died. His student Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya carried the same ruling to Jerusalem and Nablus, and the crowd there tried to kill him.

> [!note]- Taqi al-Din al-Hisni, daf' al-shubah 'an al-Rasul, p.213
> فاتفق أن ابن قيم الجوزية سافر إلى القدس الشريف ، ورقى على منبر في الحرم ووعظ ، وقال في أثناء وعظه ، بعد أن ذكر المسألة ، وقال : ها أنا راجع ، ولا أزور الخليل . ثم جاء إلى نابلس ، وعمل له مجلس وعظ ، وذكر المسألة بعينها حتى قال : فلا يزور قبر النبي ﵌ .
> فقام إليه الناس وأرادوا قتله ، فحماه منهم والي نابلس ، وكتب أهل القدس وأهل نابلس إلى دمشق يعرفون صورة ما وقع منه ، فطلبه القاضي المالكي ، فتردد ، وصعد إلى الصالحية إلى القاضي شمس الدين بن مسلم الحنبلي ، وأسلم على يديه ! فقبل توبته ، وحكم بإسلامه ، وحقن دمه ، ولم يعزره لأجل ابن تيمية . ولما كان يوم الجمعة رابع شعبان ، جلس القاضي جلال الدين بعد العصر بالمدرسة العادلية ، وأحضر جماعة من جماعة ابن تيمية كانوا معتقلين في سجن الشرع ، فادعى على إسماعيل بن كثير صاحب التاريخ أنه قال : إن التوراة والأنجيل ما بدلا ، وأنهما بحالهما كما أنزلا ، وشهدوا عليه 
>
> "It happened that Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah traveled to the noble Jerusalem. He climbed onto a pulpit in the Sanctuary and preached. During his sermon, after mentioning the issue, he said, "Here I am returning, and I will not visit al-Khalil." Then he came to Nablus, where a preaching gathering was arranged for him. He mentioned the very same issue, until he said, "One should not visit the Prophet's grave."
>
>
> The people rose against him and wanted to kill him, but the governor of Nablus protected him from them. The people of Jerusalem and the people of Nablus wrote to Damascus, reporting what had happened from him. The Maliki judge summoned him, but he hesitated. He went up to al-Salihiyyah to Judge Shams al-Din ibn Muslim the Hanbali and embraced Islam at his hands. He accepted his repentance, ruled that he was Muslim, and spared his blood. He did not discipline him on account of Ibn Taymiyyah. Then, on Friday, the fourth of Sha'ban, Judge Jalal al-Din sat after the afternoon prayer at the Adiliyyah School. He brought in a group from Ibn Taymiyyah's group who had been detained in the legal prison. He brought a claim against Isma'il ibn Kathir, the author of the history, that he had said, "The Torah and the Gospel were not altered, and they remain as they were when they were sent down." They testified against him."

Ibn Qayyim escaped with his life by submitting a renewed profession of Islam before a Hanbali judge. The historian Ibn Shakir al-Kutubi, whom al-Hisni introduces as one of Ibn Taymiyya's followers, records the same temper inside the movement itself.

> [!note]- Taqi al-Din al-Hisni, daf' al-shubah 'an al-Rasul, p.88, relaying Ibn Shakir al-Kutubi
> 
> ( تاريخ ابن تيمية كما نقله المؤرخ ابن شاكر ) وأزيد على ذلك ما ذكره صاحب ( عيون التواريخ ) ، وهو ابن شاكر ، ويعرف بصلاح الدين الكتبي وبالتريكي ، وكان من أتباع ابن تيمية ، وضرب الضرب البليغ ، لكونه قال لمؤذن في مأذنة العروس وقت السحر : أشركت ، حين قال : ألا يا رسول الله أنت وسيلتي * إلى الله في غفران ذنبي وزلتي وأرادوا ضرب عنقه ، ثم جددوا إسلامه .
> وإنما أذكر ما قاله لأنه أبلغ في حق ابن تيمية في إقامة الحجة عليه ، مع أنه أهمل أشياء من خبثه ولؤمه ، لما فيها من المبالغة في إهانة قدوته . والعجب أن ابن تيمية ذكرها ، وهو سكت عنها :
> كلام ابن تيمية في الاستواء ووثوب الناس عليه فمن ذلك ما أخبر به أبو الحسن علي الدمشقي - في صحن الجامع الأموي - عن أبيه ، قال : كنا جلوسا في مجلس ابن تيمية ، فذكر
>
> "The history of Ibn Taymiyya as transmitted by the historian Ibn Shakir. I add to this what the author of Uyun al-Tawarikh mentioned. He was Ibn Shakir, known as Salah al-Din al-Kutubi and al-Turki. He was one of Ibn Taymiyya's followers, and he was severely beaten because he said to a muezzin in the Minaret of the Bride at dawn, "You have committed associationism," when the muezzin said, "O Messenger of God, you are my means to God for the forgiveness of my sin and my lapse." They intended to strike off his neck, then they renewed his profession of Islam.
>
>
> I mention what he said only because it is more forceful regarding Ibn Taymiyya in establishing the proof against him, even though he omitted things of his malice and baseness because they contained an excessive disparagement of his exemplar. It is remarkable that Ibn Taymiyya mentioned them while he remained silent about them.
>
>
> Ibn Taymiyya's words concerning establishment and the people's rushing upon him. Among this is what Abu al-Hasan Ali al-Dimashqi reported in the courtyard of the Umayyad Mosque from his father. He said, "We were sitting in Ibn Taymiyya's gathering when he mentioned""

A muezzin called on the Prophet as his means to God, in the verse of the dawn call. Ibn Shakir told the muezzin that he had committed associationism, the sin of calling on other than God. A crowd then moved to behead Ibn Shakir, and his Islam was renewed for him. Al-Hisni, transmitting the historian roughly a century after the events, says the beating was severe and remarks that the follower softened the record out of regard for his teacher.


## Twenty-Three Years of Trials

- **Source:** al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, pp.172-175
- **Chain:** Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, from the court records and the historians of Cairo and Damascus
- **Claim:** proceedings in 705, 707, 719, 720, and 726, and the citadel death of 728

The chronology is Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani's, and it begins with an act of force. The hadith master al-Mizzi was imprisoned in Damascus, and the record of al-Durar opens Ibn Taymiyya's chain of trials with what he did about it. Ibn Taymiyya went to the prison and brought him out with his own hand.

> [!note]- Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.172
> فبلغ ابن تيمية فتوجه إلى الحبس فأخرجه بيده فبلغ القاضي فطلع إلى القلعة فوافاه ابن تيمية فتشاجرا بحضرة النائب واشتط ابن تيمية على القاضي لكون نائبه جلال الدين آذى أصحابه في غيبة النائب فامر النائب من ينادى ان من تكلم في العقائد فعل كذا به وقصد بذلك تسكين الفتنة ثم عقد لهم مجلس في سلخ رجب وجرى فيه بين
>
> "This reached Ibn Taymiyyah, so he went to the prison and brought him out with his own hand. This reached the judge, so he went up to the Citadel. Ibn Taymiyyah met him there, and they quarreled in the presence of the deputy. Ibn Taymiyyah was excessive against the judge because his deputy, Jalal al-Din, had harmed his companions during the deputy's absence. So the deputy ordered someone to announce that whoever spoke about matters of creed, such-and-such would be done to him. By this he intended to calm the disturbance. Then he convened a session for them at the end of Rajab, and there took place between"

The judge of Damascus took the matter to the citadel. Ibn Taymiyya quarreled with him in the presence of the governor's deputy. The deputy had it proclaimed that whoever spoke on the creed would be punished, to still the disturbance. The council of Rajab 705 followed. In Ramadan came the summons to Cairo.

> [!note]- Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.172

## The Verdicts of the Later School

- **Source:** Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya, pp.114-116, relayed in later works; al-Hisni, daf' al-shubah; Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, relayed by al-Hisni
- **Claim:** the later authorities itemized his contraventions and recorded verdicts from condemnation to declared unbelief

The later Shafi'i authority Ibn Hajar al-Haytami (d. 974 AH) itemized the contraventions in his collected verdicts. The list survives in relay and is quoted here as the relayers preserve it.

> [!tip]- Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya, p.116, relayed in Hasan ibn Ali al-Saqqaf, Tahnitat al-Siddiq al-Mahbub, p.49

" . 5 - وقال ابن حجر في " الفتاوى الحديثية " أيضا ص (114) :
>
> "And that the world is eternal in kind and has always been a created thing with God, so he made Him a necessary agent by His essence, not an agent by choice. Exalted is God above that. And his statement affirming corporeality, direction, movement, and that He is the size of the Throne, neither smaller nor larger. Exalted is God above this vile fabrication and manifest, explicit unbelief. . .
>
>
> 5. Ibn Hajar also said in Al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya, p. 114"

The items are the doctrine of the eternity of the world in kind and the affirmations of corporeality, direction, and transfer for God, the claims that He has a body, a direction, and movement. The list also holds the affirmation that God is the size of the Throne, neither smaller nor larger. The same authority's summary verdict survives in the edition of al-Subki's Shifa' al-Saqam. The quotation names him al-Makki, from his residence in Mecca, which is the same Ibn Hajar al-Haytami.

Against all of this stands the obituary of al-Dhahabi, his own student, which Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani transmits in full.

> [!tip]- al-Dhahabi, obituary of Ibn Taymiyya, in Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.177

>
> "I do not believe him infallible. Rather, I disagree with him on fundamental and subsidiary questions. For despite the breadth of his learning, the extent of his courage, the quick flow of his mind, and his reverence for the sanctity of religion, he was a human being. Sharpness in debate, anger, and harshness toward an opponent would come over him and create enmity for him in people's hearts. Were it not for the petulance of his opponents, he would have been a point of consensus. Their leading figures submit to his learning, acknowledge his distinctions, admit the sins of his errors, and acknowledge that he is a sea without shore and a treasure without equal. But they resent in him beliefs and actions. Every person's statement may be accepted or rejected.
>
>
> He said that he was constant in prayer and fasting and reverent toward the sacred laws inwardly and outwardly. He was not one who toyed with religion, did not single out his legal questions according to personal desire, and did not let his tongue loose with whatever occurred to him. Rather, he argued from the Qur'an, hadith, and analogy, gave proof, and debated, following the example of the imams before him. He receives one reward for his error and two rewards for his correctness. Then he said that he was ill for days in the Citadel with a severe illness until he died on the night of Monday."

Al-Dhahabi concedes the learning, the memory, the courage, and the devotion, and refuses him infallibility. He disagrees with him on fundamental and subsidiary questions. He names the sharpness in debate, the anger, and the harshness toward opponents as the traits that bred enmity toward him. He adds that his opponents' petulance kept him from being a point of consensus. He defends him from the charge of trifling with religion and of lone caprice in his rulings. He closes with his death in the citadel after a short illness. The obituary is the fairest surviving assessment by a man who knew him, and it fixes the character the councils had already met.


## What the Record Supports

The documented facts are these. The leading linguist of the age praised him and then broke with him. He ruled, in his own collected fatwas, that travel to visit the graves of the prophets is disobedience. His student Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya carried the ruling to Jerusalem and Nablus, and a crowd in Nablus tried to kill him for it. He was summoned before the judges of Egypt in 705 and 707. He signed a creed recanting the apparent-sense reading of the establishment and the descent. It was proclaimed over Damascus that whoever held his creed forfeited blood and property. He was imprisoned repeatedly across twenty-three years, the last confinement in 726 for the visitation ruling, and he died in the citadel in 728. His own student and obituarist conceded the learning and named the harshness. The later authorities of the Shafi'i school itemized his contraventions, from the eternity of the world to the attribution of body and direction to God. They recorded verdicts up to declared unbelief. A Hanbali of his own line is recorded holding that view.

The record also carries its qualifications. The minbar report is a traveler's eyewitness account with a chronological doubt attached by its own editors. The 707 recantation exists, whatever its motive. Ibn Taymiyya himself denounced as slander the summary form of the visitation charge, and his own volume holds both the ruling and the denial. The proclamation of 705 was politics as much as creed, issued in the war of the judges of Cairo. And al-Dhahabi's obituary stands as the counterweight to the verdicts, a student's defense that concedes the faults and refuses the worst. The same entry's roll of elegists keeps the mourning on the record.

The politics around the trials were real. The same record that confines him shows Shaykh Nasr al-Manbiji inciting the rulers against him over the Ibn al-Arabi letter. It shows the judges of Cairo fighting their own war through his case. Both things are in the sources. The councils that tried him were councils of his own tradition's judges. The confinement orders were the sultan's and the governor's, issued on those councils' findings, and the verdicts are the verdicts of the school's own later authorities. The career is documented, in the main, by the people who wrote the history of the tradition he belonged to.

Source. Compiled from al-Durar al-Kamina, the Rihla of Ibn Batuta, daf' al-shubah, Majmu' al-Fatawa, and the relayed verdicts of Ibn Hajar al-Haytami. Filed 2026-09-21.

blocks.text: Ibn Taymiyya on the Record of His Own School

Taqi al-Din Ahmad ibn Taymiyya (661-728 AH) is remembered today as a renewer of the Hanbali school and the ancestor of a movement. His own tradition tells a fuller story. The biographical dictionaries, travel diaries, court records, and fatwa collections document it. The writers are the scholars who sat in his circles, judged his cases, and buried him. The talent is conceded first, in the words of his own contemporaries and students. Then the record turns. The creed incidents repeatedly put him before councils of judges. The grave-visitation ruling sent him to his final prison. There is a signed recantation of 707 and a proclamation over Damascus. Later authorities of the Shafi'i school and one Hanbali of his own line also recorded verdicts against him.
Every quotation below is cited to a Sunni source. Where a report survives only in a relay, the relay is named. Where the record conflicts, the conflict is stated.
The Talent Conceded

Source: al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.178 Speaker: Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi, the era's foremost grammarian Claim: he praised Ibn Taymiyya in improvised verse, then broke with him permanently over one discourtesy about Sibawayh

Abu Hayyan of Granada met Ibn Taymiyya in Cairo and praised him in improvised verse. Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani preserves both the poem and what followed it in the authoritative biographical dictionary of the eighth century.

Abu Hayyan's praise, in Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.178 لما اتانا تقي الدين لاح لنا داع إلى اللّه فرد ما له وزر على محياه من سيما الأولى صحبوا خير البرية نور دونه القمر حبر تسربل منه دهره حبرا بحر تقاذف من أمواجه الدرر قام ابن تيمية في نصر شرعتنا مقام سيدتيم إذ عصت مضر واظهر الحق إذ آثاره اندرست واخمد الشر إذ طارت له شرر كنا نحدث عن حبر يجئ بها (1) * أنت الامام الذي قد كان ينتظر ثم دار بينهما كلام فجرى ذكر سيبويه فاغلظ ابن تيمية القول في سيبويه فنافره أبو حيان وقطعه بسببه ثم عاد ذا ماله وصير ذلك ذنبا لا يغفر قال وحج ابن المحب سنة 34 فسمع من أبى حيان انا شيد فقرأ عليه هذه الأبيات فقال قد كشطتها من ديواني ولا اذكره بخير فسأله عن السبب "When Taqi al-Din came to us, there appeared to us a caller to God, singular and bearing no burden. On his face were the marks of those who accompanied the best of created beings, a light before which the moon is dim. A learned scholar whose age clothed him in learning, a sea whose waves cast forth pearls. Ibn Taymiyya rose to support our law as Sayyid Tamim rose when Mudar rebelled. He made the truth manifest after its traces had been effaced, and he extinguished evil after its sparks had flown. We used to speak of a learned scholar who would come with it. You are the imam who had been awaited. Then words passed between them, and Sibawayh was mentioned. Ibn Taymiyya spoke harshly about Sibawayh, so Abu Hayyan broke with him and cut him off because of it. He then went back on all that he had said and made it an unforgivable sin. He said that Ibn al-Muhibb performed the pilgrimage in the year 734 and heard from Abu Hayyan that he had composed these verses. He recited them to him, and Abu Hayyan said, "I have erased them from my collected poems, and I do not mention him favorably." He asked him about the reason."

The poem is the measure of the man at his best. The same entry preserves the sequel. Words passed between the two men, the grammarian Sibawayh was mentioned, and Ibn Taymiyya spoke harshly of him. Abu Hayyan broke with him over that single discourtesy, crossed the verses out of his collected poems, and said he would not mention him favorably again. A mind that could win Abu Hayyan's verse could also lose him with a sentence.
The Minbar in Damascus

Source: Rihlat Ibn Batuta, vol.1, pp.316-317 Speaker: Ibn Batuta, who states he was present in Damascus Claim: Ibn Taymiyya illustrated the divine descent from the minbar step, a Maliki jurist who objected was beaten by the crowd, and the judges' protest reached the sultan
The traveler Ibn Batuta passed through Damascus and left a portrait in his Rihla.

Ibn Batuta, Rihlat Ibn Batuta (Tuhfat al-Nuzzar), vol.1, p.316 وكان بدمشق من كبار الفقهاء الحنابلة تقي الدين ابن تيمية (221) كبير الشأن يتكلم في الفنون إلا أن في عقله شيئا ! وكان أهل دمشق يعظمونه أشد التعظيم ويعظهم على المنبر ، وتكلم مرة بأمر أنكره الفقهاء ورفعوه إلى الملك الناصر فأمر بإشخاصه إلى القاهرة وجمع القضاة والفقهاء بمجلس الملك الناصر وتكلم شرف الدين الزواوي المالكي (222) ، وقال : إن هذا الرجل قال : كذا ، وعدّد ما أنكر على ابن تيمية ، وأحضر العقود بذلك ووضعها بين يدي قاضي القضاة وقال قاضي القضاة لابن تيمية : ما تقول ؟ قال : لا إلاه إلا الله ، فأعاد عليه فأجاب بمثل قوله ، فأمر الملك الناصر بسجنه فسجن أعواما ، وصنف في السجن كتابا "In Damascus there was among the leading Hanbali jurists Taqi al-Din Ibn Taymiyya, a man of great standing who spoke on various disciplines, except that there was something wrong with his mind. The people of Damascus held him in the highest reverence, and he preached to them from the minbar. On one occasion he spoke about a matter that the jurists condemned and brought before al-Malik al-Nasir. He ordered that Ibn Taymiyya be brought to Cairo. The judges and jurists were assembled in the council of al-Malik al-Nasir, and Sharaf al-Din al-Zawawi the Maliki spoke and said, "This man said such and such," and listed what had been condemned in Ibn Taymiyya. He produced the documents concerning this and placed them before the Chief Judge. The Chief Judge said to Ibn Taymiyya, "What do you say?" He said, "There is no god but God." He repeated the question, and Ibn Taymiyya answered in the same way. Al-Malik al-Nasir ordered him imprisoned, so he was imprisoned for years. While in prison, he composed a book."

The portrait is double-edged, and it says so itself. Ibn Taymiyya was among the leading Hanbali jurists of Damascus, a man of great standing who spoke on the sciences. There was something wrong with his mind. Ibn Batuta then records what he says he witnessed on a Friday.

Ibn Batuta, Rihlat Ibn Batuta (Tuhfat al-Nuzzar), vol.1, p.317 لاقه إلى أن وقع منه مثل ذلك ثانية ، وكنت إذ ذاك بدمشق (223) فحضرته يوم الجمعة وهو يعظ الناس على منبر الجامع ويذكّرهم فكان من جملة كلامه أن قال : إن الله ينزل إلى سماء الدنيا كنزولي هذا ، ونزل درجة من درج المنبر ، فعارضه فقيه مالكي يعرف بابن الزهراء وأنكر ما تكلم به ، فقامت العامة إلى هذا الفقيه وضربوه بالأيدي والنعال ضربا كثيرا حتى سقطت عمامته وظهر على رأسه شاشية حرير ، فأنكروا عليه لباسها واحتملوه إلى دار عز الدين بن مسلّم قاضي الحنابلة فأمر بسجنه وعزره بعد ذلك ، فأنكر فقهاء المالكية والشافعية ما كان من تعزيره ورفعوا الأمر إلى ملك الأمراء سيف الدين تنكيز (224) وكان من خيار الأمراء وصلحائهم ، فكتب إلى الملك الناصر بذلك وكتب عقدا شرعيا على ابن تيمية بأمور منكرة منها : أن المطلّق بالثلاث في كلمة واحدة لا تلزمه إلا طلقة واحدة ، (225) ومنها أن المسافر الذي ينوي بسفره زيارة القبر الشريف زاده الله طيبا لا يقصر الصلاة ، وسوى ذلك مما يشبهه ، وبعث العقد إلى الملك الناصر فأمر بسجن ابن تيمية بالقلعة فسجن بها حتى مات في السجن . ذكر مدارس دمشق إعلم أن للشافع "until the like of that occurred from him a second time. At that time I was in Damascus, and I attended him on Friday while he was preaching and reminding the people from the minbar of the congregational mosque. Among his words was his statement, "God descends to the lowest heaven as I descend in this way," and he descended one step of the minbar. A Maliki jurist known as Ibn al-Zahra objected to him and condemned what he had said. The common people rose against this jurist and struck him greatly with their hands and sandals until his turban fell off and a silk cap appeared on his head. They condemned him for wearing it and carried him to the house of Izz al-Din Ibn Muslim, the Hanbali judge. He ordered him imprisoned and afterward disciplined him. The Maliki and Shafi'i jurists condemned his having been disciplined and referred the matter to the commander of the emirs, Sayf al-Din Tankiz, who was among the best and most righteous of the emirs. He wrote to al-Malik al-Nasir about this and drew up a legal document against Ibn Taymiyya concerning objectionable matters, among them that a man who pronounces a threefold divorce in one utterance incurs only one divorce, and among them that a traveler whose purpose in traveling is to visit the Noble Grave, may God increase it in goodness, does not shorten the prayer, along with other similar matters. He sent the document to al-Malik al-Nasir, who ordered Ibn Taymiyya imprisoned in the Citadel. He remained imprisoned there until he died in prison. Mention of the schools of Damascus Know that the Shafi'is"

On this report, Ibn Taymiyya, preaching on the descent of God, descended one step of the minbar to illustrate the manner of the descent. The Maliki jurist Ibn al-Zahra objected from the congregation. The crowd beat the objector with hands and sandals until his turban fell. The Hanbali judge of Damascus then imprisoned the objector and had him disciplined. The Maliki and Shafi'i jurists carried the protest to the governor of Syria, Tankiz. The modern editors of the Rihla note a chronological difficulty in the report. One commentator suggested the scribe embellished it. The report stands as the traveler recorded it, with that doubt attached.
The Ruling on Visiting Graves

Source: Majmu' al-Fatawa, vol.27, p.27 Speaker: Ibn Taymiyya, citing Ibn Aqil and a group of the scholars Claim: travel to visit the graves of the prophets is disobedience, and the traveler does not shorten his prayer on that journey
The ruling that put Ibn Taymiyya in his final prison was his own, recorded in his own collected fatwas.

Ibn Taymiyya, Majmu' al-Fatawa, vol.27, p.27 بِأَنَّ الْمُسَافِرَ لِزِيَارَةِ قُبُورِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ عَلَيْهِمْ السَّلَامُ وَغَيْرِهَا لَا يَقْصُرُ الصَّلَاةَ فِي هَذَا السَّفَرِ ؛ لِأَنَّهُ مَعْصِيَةٌ لِكَوْنِهِ مُعْتَقِداً أَنَّهُ طَاعَةٌ وَلَيْسَ بِطَاعَةِ وَالتَّقَرُّبُ إلَى اللَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ بِمَا لَيْسَ بِطَاعَةِ هُوَ مَعْصِيَةٌ ؛ وَلِأَنَّهُ نَهَى عَنْ ذَلِكَ وَالنَّهْيُ يَقْتَضِي التَّحْرِيمَ . وَرَخَّصَ بَعْضُ الْمُتَأَخِّرِينَ فِي السَّفَرِ لِزِيَارَةِ الْقُبُورِ كَمَا ذَكَرَ أَبُو "A traveler who travels to visit the graves of the prophets, peace be upon them, and others does not shorten the prayer during this journey, because it is a sin. This is because he believes it to be an act of obedience, when it is not an act of obedience. Seeking nearness to God, Mighty and Majestic, through what is not an act of obedience is a sin. It is also because he prohibited that, and a prohibition entails forbiddance. Some later scholars permitted traveling to visit graves, as Abu mentioned"

The reasoning is stated plainly. A traveler who sets out to visit the graves of the prophets believes he is performing an act of obedience, and the act is not one. Seeking nearness to God through what is not obedience is disobedience, and the prohibition entails forbiddance. Ibn Taymiyya cites earlier authorities for the ruling and notes that some later scholars permitted the travel. The Arabic excerpt breaks off inside the name of Ibn Aqil, the authority the fatwa is citing. Elsewhere in the same volume, in the passage at vol.27, p.253, he denounces as slander the summary claim that he forbids visiting the Prophet's grave and traveling to it. Both texts are his. On this record the operative ruling is the first, and the governor's dossier itemized it when the final imprisonment came.

Ibn Batuta, Rihlat Ibn Batuta, vol.1, p.317 فكتب إلى الملك الناصر بذلك وكتب عقدا شرعيا على ابن تيمية بأمور منكرة منها : أن المطلّق بالثلاث في كلمة واحدة لا تلزمه إلا طلقة واحدة ، (225) ومنها أن المسافر الذي ينوي بسفره زيارة القبر الشريف زاده الله طيبا لا يقصر الصلاة ، وسوى ذلك مما يشبهه ، وبعث العقد إلى الملك الناصر فأمر بسجن ابن تيمية بالقلعة فسجن بها حتى مات في السجن . ذكر مدارس دمشق إعلم أن للشافعية بدمشق جملة من المدارس أعظمها العادلية (226) ، وبها يحكم قاضي القضاة ، وتقابلها المدرسة الظاهرية (227) وبها قبر الملك الظاهر ، وبها جلوس نواب "He wrote to al-Malik al-Nasir about this and drew up a legal document against Ibn Taymiyya concerning objectionable matters, among them that a man who pronounces a threefold divorce in one utterance incurs only one divorce, and among them that a traveler whose purpose in traveling is to visit the Noble Grave, may God increase it in goodness, does not shorten the prayer, along with other similar matters. He sent the document to al-Malik al-Nasir, who ordered Ibn Taymiyya imprisoned in the Citadel. He remained imprisoned there until he died in prison. Mention of the schools of Damascus Know that the Shafi'is in Damascus have a number of schools, the greatest of which is the Adiliyya. The Chief Judge gives judgment there. Opposite it is the Zahariyya school, in which is the grave of al-Malik al-Zahir, and there is the seat of the deputies"

The dossier Tankiz, governor of Syria, sent to Sultan al-Nasir named the rulings as errors. The threefold divorce counted as one. The pilgrim who intends the visit of the grave does not shorten his prayer. The order that followed confined Ibn Taymiyya to the citadel of Damascus, where he remained until he died. His student Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya carried the same ruling to Jerusalem and Nablus, and the crowd there tried to kill him.

Taqi al-Din al-Hisni, daf' al-shubah 'an al-Rasul, p.213 فاتفق أن ابن قيم الجوزية سافر إلى القدس الشريف ، ورقى على منبر في الحرم ووعظ ، وقال في أثناء وعظه ، بعد أن ذكر المسألة ، وقال : ها أنا راجع ، ولا أزور الخليل . ثم جاء إلى نابلس ، وعمل له مجلس وعظ ، وذكر المسألة بعينها حتى قال : فلا يزور قبر النبي ﵌ . فقام إليه الناس وأرادوا قتله ، فحماه منهم والي نابلس ، وكتب أهل القدس وأهل نابلس إلى دمشق يعرفون صورة ما وقع منه ، فطلبه القاضي المالكي ، فتردد ، وصعد إلى الصالحية إلى القاضي شمس الدين بن مسلم الحنبلي ، وأسلم على يديه ! فقبل توبته ، وحكم بإسلامه ، وحقن دمه ، ولم يعزره لأجل ابن تيمية . ولما كان يوم الجمعة رابع شعبان ، جلس القاضي جلال الدين بعد العصر بالمدرسة العادلية ، وأحضر جماعة من جماعة ابن تيمية كانوا معتقلين في سجن الشرع ، فادعى على إسماعيل بن كثير صاحب التاريخ أنه قال : إن التوراة والأنجيل ما بدلا ، وأنهما بحالهما كما أنزلا ، وشهدوا عليه "It happened that Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyyah traveled to the noble Jerusalem. He climbed onto a pulpit in the Sanctuary and preached. During his sermon, after mentioning the issue, he said, "Here I am returning, and I will not visit al-Khalil." Then he came to Nablus, where a preaching gathering was arranged for him. He mentioned the very same issue, until he said, "One should not visit the Prophet's grave." The people rose against him and wanted to kill him, but the governor of Nablus protected him from them. The people of Jerusalem and the people of Nablus wrote to Damascus, reporting what had happened from him. The Maliki judge summoned him, but he hesitated. He went up to al-Salihiyyah to Judge Shams al-Din ibn Muslim the Hanbali and embraced Islam at his hands. He accepted his repentance, ruled that he was Muslim, and spared his blood. He did not discipline him on account of Ibn Taymiyyah. Then, on Friday, the fourth of Sha'ban, Judge Jalal al-Din sat after the afternoon prayer at the Adiliyyah School. He brought in a group from Ibn Taymiyyah's group who had been detained in the legal prison. He brought a claim against Isma'il ibn Kathir, the author of the history, that he had said, "The Torah and the Gospel were not altered, and they remain as they were when they were sent down." They testified against him."

Ibn Qayyim escaped with his life by submitting a renewed profession of Islam before a Hanbali judge. The historian Ibn Shakir al-Kutubi, whom al-Hisni introduces as one of Ibn Taymiyya's followers, records the same temper inside the movement itself.

Taqi al-Din al-Hisni, daf' al-shubah 'an al-Rasul, p.88, relaying Ibn Shakir al-Kutubi ( تاريخ ابن تيمية كما نقله المؤرخ ابن شاكر ) وأزيد على ذلك ما ذكره صاحب ( عيون التواريخ ) ، وهو ابن شاكر ، ويعرف بصلاح الدين الكتبي وبالتريكي ، وكان من أتباع ابن تيمية ، وضرب الضرب البليغ ، لكونه قال لمؤذن في مأذنة العروس وقت السحر : أشركت ، حين قال : ألا يا رسول الله أنت وسيلتي * إلى الله في غفران ذنبي وزلتي وأرادوا ضرب عنقه ، ثم جددوا إسلامه . وإنما أذكر ما قاله لأنه أبلغ في حق ابن تيمية في إقامة الحجة عليه ، مع أنه أهمل أشياء من خبثه ولؤمه ، لما فيها من المبالغة في إهانة قدوته . والعجب أن ابن تيمية ذكرها ، وهو سكت عنها : كلام ابن تيمية في الاستواء ووثوب الناس عليه فمن ذلك ما أخبر به أبو الحسن علي الدمشقي - في صحن الجامع الأموي - عن أبيه ، قال : كنا جلوسا في مجلس ابن تيمية ، فذكر "The history of Ibn Taymiyya as transmitted by the historian Ibn Shakir. I add to this what the author of Uyun al-Tawarikh mentioned. He was Ibn Shakir, known as Salah al-Din al-Kutubi and al-Turki. He was one of Ibn Taymiyya's followers, and he was severely beaten because he said to a muezzin in the Minaret of the Bride at dawn, "You have committed associationism," when the muezzin said, "O Messenger of God, you are my means to God for the forgiveness of my sin and my lapse." They intended to strike off his neck, then they renewed his profession of Islam. I mention what he said only because it is more forceful regarding Ibn Taymiyya in establishing the proof against him, even though he omitted things of his malice and baseness because they contained an excessive disparagement of his exemplar. It is remarkable that Ibn Taymiyya mentioned them while he remained silent about them. Ibn Taymiyya's words concerning establishment and the people's rushing upon him. Among this is what Abu al-Hasan Ali al-Dimashqi reported in the courtyard of the Umayyad Mosque from his father. He said, "We were sitting in Ibn Taymiyya's gathering when he mentioned""

A muezzin called on the Prophet as his means to God, in the verse of the dawn call. Ibn Shakir told the muezzin that he had committed associationism, the sin of calling on other than God. A crowd then moved to behead Ibn Shakir, and his Islam was renewed for him. Al-Hisni, transmitting the historian roughly a century after the events, says the beating was severe and remarks that the follower softened the record out of regard for his teacher.
Twenty-Three Years of Trials

Source: al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, pp.172-175 Chain: Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, from the court records and the historians of Cairo and Damascus Claim: proceedings in 705, 707, 719, 720, and 726, and the citadel death of 728

The chronology is Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani's, and it begins with an act of force. The hadith master al-Mizzi was imprisoned in Damascus, and the record of al-Durar opens Ibn Taymiyya's chain of trials with what he did about it. Ibn Taymiyya went to the prison and brought him out with his own hand.

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.172 فبلغ ابن تيمية فتوجه إلى الحبس فأخرجه بيده فبلغ القاضي فطلع إلى القلعة فوافاه ابن تيمية فتشاجرا بحضرة النائب واشتط ابن تيمية على القاضي لكون نائبه جلال الدين آذى أصحابه في غيبة النائب فامر النائب من ينادى ان من تكلم في العقائد فعل كذا به وقصد بذلك تسكين الفتنة ثم عقد لهم مجلس في سلخ رجب وجرى فيه بين "This reached Ibn Taymiyyah, so he went to the prison and brought him out with his own hand. This reached the judge, so he went up to the Citadel. Ibn Taymiyyah met him there, and they quarreled in the presence of the deputy. Ibn Taymiyyah was excessive against the judge because his deputy, Jalal al-Din, had harmed his companions during the deputy's absence. So the deputy ordered someone to announce that whoever spoke about matters of creed, such-and-such would be done to him. By this he intended to calm the disturbance. Then he convened a session for them at the end of Rajab, and there took place between"

The judge of Damascus took the matter to the citadel. Ibn Taymiyya quarreled with him in the presence of the governor's deputy. The deputy had it proclaimed that whoever spoke on the creed would be punished, to still the disturbance. The council of Rajab 705 followed. In Ramadan came the summons to Cairo.

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.172 وعقد مجلس في ثالث عشر (3) منه بعد صلاة الجمعة فادعى على ابن تيمية عند المالكي فقال هذا عدوى ولم يجب عن الدعوى فكرر "A council was convened on the thirteenth of that month after the Friday prayer. A claim was brought against Ibn Taymiyya before the Maliki judge. He said, "This is my enemy," and did not answer the claim. It was repeated"
Before the Maliki judge of Egypt the claim against him was read, and he would not answer it. The ruling and proclamation that followed are Ibn Hajar's to transmit.

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.173 بسه فأقيم من المجلس وحبس في برج ثم بلغ الملكي ان الناس يترددون اليه فقال يجب التضييق عليه ان لم يقتل والا فقد ثبت كفره فنقلوه ليلة عيد الفطر إلى الجب وعاد القاضي الشافعي إلى ولايته ونودي بدمشق من اعتقد عقيدة ابن تيمية حل دمه وماله خصوصا الحنابلة فنودي بذلك وقرئ المرسوم وقرأها ابن الشهاب محمود في الجامع ثم جمعوا الحنابلة من الصالحية وغيرها واشهدوا على أنفسهم انهم على معتقد الامام الشافعي وذكر ولد الشيخ جمال الدين ابن الظاهري في كتاب كتبه لبعض معارفه بدمشق ان جميع من بمصر من القضاة والشيوخ والفقراء والعلماء والعوام يحطون على ابن تيمية الا الحنفي فإنه يتعصب له والا الشافعي فإنه ساكت عنه وكان من أعظم القائمين عليه الشيخ نصر المنبجى لأنه كان بلغ ابن تيمية انه يتعصب لابن العربي فكتب اليه كتابا يعاتبه على ذلك فما اعجبه لكونه بالغ في الحط على ابن العربي وتكفيره فصار هو يحط على ابن تيمية ويغرى به بيبرس الجاشنكير وكان بيبرس يفرط في محبة نصر ( ويعظمه وقام القاضي زي "He was removed from the council and imprisoned in a tower. Then the Maliki was told that people were visiting him, and he said, "He must be kept under tighter confinement if he is not killed. Otherwise, his unbelief has been established." They moved him on the night of Eid al-Fitr to the pit. The Shafi'i judge returned to his office. A proclamation was made in Damascus that whoever held Ibn Taymiyya's creed, especially the Hanbalis, had made his blood and property lawful. This was proclaimed, the decree was read, and Ibn al-Shihab Mahmud read it in the congregational mosque. Then they gathered the Hanbalis from al-Salihiyya and elsewhere and made them testify against themselves that they followed the creed of Imam al-Shafi'i. The son of Shaykh Jamal al-Din ibn al-Zahiri mentioned in a book that he wrote to one of his acquaintances in Damascus that everyone in Egypt among the judges, shaykhs, poor ascetics, scholars, and common people disparaged Ibn Taymiyya, except the Hanafi, who was partisan toward him, and the Shafi'i, who remained silent about him. Among those most active against him was Shaykh Nasr al-Manbaji, because Ibn Taymiyya had learned that he was partisan toward Ibn al-Arabi. So he wrote him a letter reproaching him for that. Nasr did not like it, because Ibn Taymiyya had gone to extremes in disparaging Ibn al-Arabi and declaring him an unbeliever. Thus Nasr began to disparage Ibn Taymiyya and incite Baybars al-Jashankir against him. Baybars was excessive in his love for Nasr and held him in high esteem. Qadi Zay"

The Maliki judge held that his disbelief was established and that he must be confined if not killed. A proclamation ran over Damascus that whoever held Ibn Taymiyya's creed had forfeited his blood and property. The Hanbalis of al-Salihiyya were assembled to testify against themselves that they held the creed of al-Shafi'i. In 707, in Cairo, Ibn Taymiyya signed the document drawn against him.

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.174 فكتب عليه محضر بأنه قال انا اشعرى ثم وجد خطه بما نصه الذي اعتقد ان القرآن معنى قائم بذات اللّه وهو صفة من صفات ذاته القديمة وهو غير مخلوق وليس بحرف ولا صوت وان قوله الرحمن على العرش استوى ليس على ظاهره ولا اعلم كنه المراد به بل لا يعلمه الا اللّه والقول في النزول كالقول في الاستواء وكتبه أحمد بن تيمية ثم اشهدوا عليه انه تاب مما ينافي ذلك مختار أو ذلك في خامس عشرى ربيع الأول سنة 707 وشهد عليه بذلك جمع جم من العلماء وغيرهم وسكن الحال وافرج عنه وسكن القاهرة ثم اجتمع جمع من الصوفية عند تاج الدين ابن عطاء فطلعوا في العشر الأوسط من شوال إلى القلعة وشكوا من ابن تيمية انه يتكلم في حق مشايخ الطريق وأنه قال لا يستغاث بالنبي صلّى اللّه عليه وسلم فاقتضى الحال ان امر بتسييره إلى الشام فتوجه على خيل البريد . . . (1) وكل ذلك والقاضي زين الدين ابن مخلوف مشتغل بنفسه بالمرض وقد اشرف على الموت وبلغه سفر ابن تيمية فراسل النائب فرده من بلبيس وادعى عليه عند ابن جماعة وشهد عليه شرف الدين ابن الصابوني وقيل إن علاء الدين القونوى أيضا "A document was written against him stating that he had said, "I am an Ash'ari." Then his handwriting was found containing the following text. "What I believe is that the Qur'an is a meaning subsisting in the essence of God. It is one of the attributes of His eternal essence. It is uncreated, and it is neither letter nor sound. His saying, 'The Most Merciful established Himself over the Throne,' is not according to its apparent sense, and I do not know the true nature of what is meant by it. Rather, no one knows it except God. The statement concerning descent is like the statement concerning establishment." It was written by Ahmad ibn Taymiyya. They then made him testify that he had repented from what contradicted this voluntarily. That was on the fifteenth of Rabi al-Awwal in the year 707. A large group of scholars and others testified to this against him. The matter became quiet, he was released, and he resided in Cairo. Then a group of Sufis gathered with Taj al-Din Ibn Ata. During the middle ten days of Shawwal, they went up to the Citadel and complained about Ibn Taymiyya, saying that he spoke concerning the shaykhs of the path and that he had said, "The Prophet is not to be appealed to for rescue." The circumstances required that he be ordered to be sent to Syria, so he set out on the postal mounts. . . . All this took place while Judge Zayn al-Din Ibn Makhluf was occupied with his illness and had come close to death. News of Ibn Taymiyya's departure reached him, so he sent a message to the deputy, who brought him back from Bilbays. He brought a claim against him before Ibn Jama'a, and Sharaf al-Din Ibn al-Sabuni testified against him. It was also said that Ala al-Din al-Qunawi did so."

The signed creed affirms that the Qur'an is neither letter nor sound. It affirms that the establishment over the Throne is not according to its apparent sense, and that the statement concerning descent is like the statement concerning establishment. The creed he was made to sign was the Ash'ari one, the theology of the kalam school that his Hanbali circle opposed, and the document marks how far the concession went. The witnesses certified his repentance from whatever contradicted it. Later that same year the Sufis of Cairo complained to the citadel. They said he spoke against the masters of the path and taught that no aid is sought from the Prophet. He was sent back toward Syria. The chain then runs unbroken through Ibn Hajar's record.

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.175 ثم قاموا عليه في شهر رمضان سنة 719 بسبب مسألة الطلاق واكد عليه المنع من الفتيا ثم عقد له مجلس آخر في رجب سنة عشرين ثم حبس بالقلعة ثم اخرج في عاشوراء سنة 721 ثم قاموا عليه مرة أخرى في شعبان سنة 726 بسبب مسألة الزيارة واعتقل بالقلعة فلم يزل بها إلى أن مات في ليلة الاثنين العشرين من ذي القعدة سنة 728 قال الصلاح الصفدي كان كثيرا ما ينشد تموت النفوس باوصابها ولم تدر عوادها مابها "Then they proceeded against him in Ramadan of the year 719 because of the question of divorce, and the prohibition against his issuing legal opinions was made more stringent. Then another council was convened for him in Rajab of the year 720, and he was imprisoned in the Citadel. He was then released on Ashura of the year 721. Then they proceeded against him once more in Shaban of the year 726 because of the question of visitation, and he was detained in the Citadel. He remained there until he died on the night of Monday, the twentieth of Dhu al-Qada, in the year 728. Salah al-Din al-Safadi said that he often recited, "Souls die from their pains, while those who visit them do not know what is in them.""

Ramadan 719, the divorce ruling, and a stringent prohibition on his legal opinions. Rajab 720, another council, the citadel. 721, release. Shaban 726, the visitation ruling, the citadel again, and there he stayed until his death on the night of Monday, the twentieth of Dhu al-Qa'da 728. Ibn Hajar's informant on the mood of Egypt confirms the isolation.
The same entry closes its account of his death with a roll of the poets who elegized him.

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.176 قال ورثاه محمود بن علي الدقوقى ومجير الدين ابن الخياط وصفى الدين عبد المؤمن البغدادي وجمال الدين ابن الأثير وتقى الدين محمد ابن سليمان الجعبرى وعلاء الدين بن غانم وشهاب الدين ابن فضل اللّه وزين الدين ابن الوردي وجمع جم "He said that he was elegized by Mahmud ibn Ali al-Duquqi, Mujir al-Din ibn al-Khayyat, Safi al-Din Abd al-Mumin al-Baghdadi, Jamal al-Din ibn al-Athir, Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Jabari, Ala al-Din ibn Ghanim, Shihab al-Din ibn Fadl Allah, and Zayn al-Din ibn al-Wardi, and a great multitude."
Eight poets are named, and the entry adds a great multitude beyond them. Whatever the councils judged, the school's own biographical dictionary records him mourned in verse.

Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.173 ان جميع من بمصر من القضاة والشيوخ والفقراء والعلماء والعوام يحطون على ابن تيمية الا الحنفي فإنه يتعصب له والا الشافعي فإنه ساكت عنه وكان من أعظم القائمين عليه الشيخ نصر المنبجى لأنه كان بلغ ابن تيمية انه يتعصب لابن العربي فكتب اليه كتابا يعاتبه على ذلك فما اعجبه لكونه بالغ في الحط على ابن العربي وتكفيره فصار هو يحط على ابن تيمية ويغرى به بيبرس الجاشنكير وكان بيبرس يفرط في محبة نصر ( ويعظمه وقام القاضي زين الدين ابن مخلوف قاضى المالكية مع الشيخ نصر ) (2) وبالغ في أذية الحنابلة واتفق ان قاضى الحنابلة شرف الدين الحراني كان قليل البضاعة في العلم فبادر إلى اجابتهم في المعتقد واستكتبوه خطه بذلك واتفق ان قاضى الحنفية بدمشق وهو شمس الدين ان الحريري انتصر لابن تيمية وكتب في حقه محضرا بالثناء عليه بال "All those in Egypt among the judges, shaykhs, poor Sufis, scholars, and common people spoke against Ibn Taymiyya, except for the Hanafi, who was partisan toward him, and the Shafi'i, who remained silent about him. Among those most active against him was Shaykh Nasr al-Manbiji. Ibn Taymiyya had learned that he was partisan toward Ibn al-Arabi, so he wrote him a letter reproaching him for that. It did not please Nasr because Ibn Taymiyya had gone to extremes in disparaging Ibn al-Arabi and declaring him an unbeliever. Nasr therefore began to disparage Ibn Taymiyya and incite Baybars al-Jashankir against him. Baybars was excessive in his love for Nasr and in honoring him. Judge Zayn al-Din Ibn Makhluf, the Maliki judge, joined Shaykh Nasr and went to extremes in harming the Hanbalis. It happened that Sharaf al-Din al-Harrani, the Hanbali judge, had little learning, so he hastened to answer them concerning the creed, and they had him write out his statement on it in his own hand. It also happened that the Hanafi judge of Damascus, Shams al-Din al-Hariri, defended Ibn Taymiyya and wrote a document in praise of him with"

All those in Egypt, judges, shaykhs, Sufis, scholars, and the common people, spoke against him, the Hanafi excepted as his partisan, the Shafi'i as silent. In Damascus the Hanafi judge Shams al-Din al-Hariri defended him and wrote a document in his praise.
The Verdicts of the Later School

Source: Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya, pp.114-116, relayed in later works; al-Hisni, daf' al-shubah; Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, relayed by al-Hisni Claim: the later authorities itemized his contraventions and recorded verdicts from condemnation to declared unbelief
The later Shafi'i authority Ibn Hajar al-Haytami (d. 974 AH) itemized the contraventions in his collected verdicts. The list survives in relay and is quoted here as the relayers preserve it.

Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya, p.116, relayed in Hasan ibn Ali al-Saqqaf, Tahnitat al-Siddiq al-Mahbub, p.49 وأن العالم قديم بالنوع ولم يزل مع الله مخلوقا دائما فجعله موجبا بالذات لا فاعلا بالاختيار تعالى الله عن ذلك ، وقوله بالجسمية ، والجهة ، والانتقال ، وأنه بقدر العرش لا أصغر ولا أكبر ، تعالى الله عن هذا الافتراء الشنيع والكفر البواح الصريح . . " . 5 - وقال ابن حجر في " الفتاوى الحديثية " أيضا ص (114) : "And that the world is eternal in kind and has always been a created thing with God, so he made Him a necessary agent by His essence, not an agent by choice. Exalted is God above that. And his statement affirming corporeality, direction, movement, and that He is the size of the Throne, neither smaller nor larger. Exalted is God above this vile fabrication and manifest, explicit unbelief. . . Ibn Hajar also said in Al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya, p. 114"

The items are the doctrine of the eternity of the world in kind and the affirmations of corporeality, direction, and transfer for God, the claims that He has a body, a direction, and movement. The list also holds the affirmation that God is the size of the Throne, neither smaller nor larger. The same authority's summary verdict survives in the edition of al-Subki's Shifa' al-Saqam. The quotation names him al-Makki, from his residence in Mecca, which is the same Ibn Hajar al-Haytami.

Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya, quoted in the edition of al-Subki, Shifa' al-Saqam, p.38 المكي في الفتاوى الحديثية ، ما نصه : ابن تيمية عبد خذله الله وأضله وأعماه وأصمه وأذله ، وبذلك صرح الأئمة الذين بينوا فساد أحواله ، وكذب أقواله ، ومن أراد ذلك فعليه بمطالعة كلام الإمام المجتهد المتفق على إمامته وبلاغه رتبة الاجتهاد أبي الحسن السبكي ، وولده التاج (5) . قال الإمام محمد بخيت المطيعي شيخ الإسلام : ولما تظاهر قوم في هذا العصر بتقليد ابن تيمية في عقائده الكاسدة وتعضيد أقواله الفاسدة . . . وجدنا كتاب الإمام الجليل والمجتهد الك "Al-Makki wrote in al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyya as follows. Ibn Taymiyya was a servant whom God forsook, led astray, blinded, deafened, and humiliated. The imams who explained the corruption of his condition and the falsity of his statements explicitly said this. Whoever wishes to know this should consult the words of the imam, mujtahid, and universally acknowledged imam, Abu al-Hasan al-Subki, who attained the rank of ijtihad, and of his son Taj. Imam Muhammad Bakhit al-Muti'i, Shaykh al-Islam, said. When some people in this age openly imitated Ibn Taymiyya in his stagnant beliefs and supported his corrupt statements, we found the book of the eminent imam and mujtahid al-ka"

Al-Hisni of Damascus, a century closer to the events than al-Haytami, wrote his book to answer the visitation rulings, and he writes as an open partisan of that cause. His verdict is categorical, and he states it as his own verdict, not as a finding.

Taqi al-Din al-Hisni, daf' al-shubah 'an al-Rasul, p.184 ابن تيمية من أعظم الكذبة والفجار) وإذا تقرر ذلك ، ففي ذكري ما أتبرع به - مع غاية الاقتصار - تتحقق أن ابن تيمية من أعظم الكذبة والفجار ، وقد انكشف لك ذلك كما انكشف ضوء النهار : فمن ذلك ما ذكره القاضي أبو الطيب - وهو من أئمة الشافعية - قال : ويستحب أن يزور قبر النبي ﵌ بعد أن يحج ويعتمر . وكيف يزور من غير سفر ، سواء كان راكبا أو ماشيا ؟ ! وقال المحاملي في كتابه (التجريد) ويستحب للحاج إذا فرغ من مكة أن يزور قبر النبي ﵌ انتهى . وقال الحليمي في كتابه (المنهاج) ، عند ذكر تعظيم النبي ﵌ ، وذكر جملة ، ثم "Ibn Taymiyyah is among the greatest liars and wicked people. Once that is established, then by mentioning what I will contribute, with the utmost brevity, you will realize that Ibn Taymiyyah is among the greatest liars and wicked people. This has become clear to you as the light of day becomes clear. Among this is what Judge Abu al-Tayyib, one of the leading Shafi'i scholars, mentioned. He said, "It is recommended that one visit the Prophet's grave after performing the pilgrimage and the lesser pilgrimage." How could one visit without traveling, whether riding or walking? Al-Mahamili said in his book al-Tajrid, "It is recommended for a pilgrim, once he has finished in Mecca, to visit the Prophet's grave." End quote. Al-Halimi said in his book al-Minhaj, when discussing the veneration of the Prophet, and he mentioned a number of matters, then"
He builds it from a run of Shafi'i authorities on the visitation, from al-Qadi Abu al-Tayyib to al-Mahamili to al-Halimi. A Hanbali of the following generation held the darker view.

Taqi al-Din al-Hisni, daf' al-shubah 'an al-Rasul, p.214, on Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali ابن رجب الحنبلي يكفر ابن تيمية ) وكان الشيخ زين الدين ابن رجب الحنبلي ممن يعتقد كفر ابن تيمية ، وله عليه "Ibn Rajab the Hanbali declares Ibn Taymiyya an unbeliever. Shaykh Zayn al-Din Ibn Rajab the Hanbali was among those who believed Ibn Taymiyya to be an unbeliever, and he had against him"

Ibn Rajab al-Hanbali, of Ibn Taymiyya's own school two generations later, is recorded by al-Hisni among those who believed him an unbeliever. The entry breaks off at that point in the printed text. Against all of this stands the obituary of al-Dhahabi, his own student, which Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani transmits in full.

al-Dhahabi, obituary of Ibn Taymiyya, in Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, al-Durar al-Kamina, vol.1, p.177 وانا لا اعتقد فيه عصمة بل انا مخالف له في مسائل أصلية وفرعية فإنه كان مع سعة علمه وفرط شجاعته وسيلان ذهنه وتعظيمه لحرمان (1) الدين بشرا من البشر تعتريه حدة في البحث وغضب وشظف للخصم تذرع (2) له عداوة في النفوس والا لولا طف خصومه لكان كلمة اجماع فان كبارهم خاضعون لعلومه معترفون بشنوفه (3) مقرون بنذور (4) خطائه وانه بحر لا ساحل له وكنز لا نظير له ولكن ينقمون عليه اخلافا (5) وافعالا وكل أحد يؤخذ من قوله ويترك * قال وكان محافظا على الصلاة والصوم معظما للشرائع ظاهرا وباطنا لا يؤتى من سوء فهم فان له الذكاء المفرط ولا من قلة علم فإنه بحر زخار ولا كان متلاعبا بالدين ولا ينفرد بمسائله بالتشهى ولا يطلق لسانه بما اتفق بل يحتج بالقرآن والحديث والقياس ويبرهن ويناظر أسوة من تقدمه من الأئمة فله اجر على خطائه واجران على اصابته إلى أن قال تمرض أياما بالقلعة بمرض جد إلى أن مات ليلة الاثنين "I do not believe him infallible. Rather, I disagree with him on fundamental and subsidiary questions. For despite the breadth of his learning, the extent of his courage, the quick flow of his mind, and his reverence for the sanctity of religion, he was a human being. Sharpness in debate, anger, and harshness toward an opponent would come over him and create enmity for him in people's hearts. Were it not for the petulance of his opponents, he would have been a point of consensus. Their leading figures submit to his learning, acknowledge his distinctions, admit the sins of his errors, and acknowledge that he is a sea without shore and a treasure without equal. But they resent in him beliefs and actions. Every person's statement may be accepted or rejected. He said that he was constant in prayer and fasting and reverent toward the sacred laws inwardly and outwardly. He was not to be faulted for poor understanding, for he possessed extraordinary intelligence, nor for lack of knowledge, for he was a surging sea. He was not one who toyed with religion, did not single out his legal questions according to personal desire, and did not let his tongue loose with whatever occurred to him. Rather, he argued from the Qur'an, hadith, and analogy, gave proof, and debated, following the example of the imams before him. He receives one reward for his error and two rewards for his correctness. Then he said that he was ill for days in the Citadel with a severe illness until he died on the night of Monday."

Al-Dhahabi concedes the learning, the memory, the courage, and the devotion, and refuses him infallibility. He disagrees with him on fundamental and subsidiary questions. He names the sharpness in debate, the anger, and the harshness toward opponents as the traits that bred enmity toward him. He adds that his opponents' petulance kept him from being a point of consensus. He defends him from the charge of trifling with religion and of lone caprice in his rulings. He closes with his death in the citadel after a short illness. The obituary is the fairest surviving assessment by a man who knew him, and it fixes the character the councils had already met.
What the Record Supports

The documented facts are these. The leading linguist of the age praised him and then broke with him. He ruled, in his own collected fatwas, that travel to visit the graves of the prophets is disobedience. His student Ibn Qayyim al-Jawziyya carried the ruling to Jerusalem and Nablus, and a crowd in Nablus tried to kill him for it. He was summoned before the judges of Egypt in 705 and 707. He signed a creed recanting the apparent-sense reading of the establishment and the descent. It was proclaimed over Damascus that whoever held his creed forfeited blood and property. He was imprisoned repeatedly across twenty-three years, the last confinement in 726 for the visitation ruling, and he died in the citadel in 728. His own student and obituarist conceded the learning and named the harshness. The later authorities of the Shafi'i school itemized his contraventions, from the eternity of the world to the attribution of body and direction to God. They recorded verdicts up to declared unbelief. A Hanbali of his own line is recorded holding that view.

The record also carries its qualifications. The minbar report is a traveler's eyewitness account with a chronological doubt attached by its own editors. The 707 recantation exists, whatever its motive. Ibn Taymiyya himself denounced as slander the summary form of the visitation charge, and his own volume holds both the ruling and the denial. The proclamation of 705 was politics as much as creed, issued in the war of the judges of Cairo. And al-Dhahabi's obituary stands as the counterweight to the verdicts, a student's defense that concedes the faults and refuses the worst. The same entry's roll of elegists keeps the mourning on the record.

The politics around the trials were real. The same record that confines him shows Shaykh Nasr al-Manbiji inciting the rulers against him over the Ibn al-Arabi letter. It shows the judges of Cairo fighting their own war through his case. Both things are in the sources. The councils that tried him were councils of his own tradition's judges. The confinement orders were the sultan's and the governor's, issued on those councils' findings, and the verdicts are the verdicts of the school's own later authorities. The career is documented, in the main, by the people who wrote the history of the tradition he belonged to.
